utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usual routine. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Anna Richterova for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Richterova. And appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Milan Trbojevic, co-counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Lead counsel Mr. Ackerman is with us and our assistant Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for General Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau and I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, madam. So any preliminaries? The request for the Chamber to go into closed session still stands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it is the same situation as yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know that. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm presuming, and probably correctly, that the Chamber would not entertain a motion for adjournment in honour of the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I was on the phone with my family just a few minutes ago. My two daughters, who are both lawyers, didn't go to court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My son-in-law, who is also a lawyer, didn't either. My other daughter's boyfriend is also watching the football matches. My wife has joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm the only one who's working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You could fire a cannon up the streets here in The Hague today and not hit anybody today. Nobody is working except us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Ackerman, it's important that we go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would love to be watching the match, but duty comes first. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope you didn't take me seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not. I think we need to prepare the courtroom to go into closed session. The members of the -- in the public gallery need to understand we have a delicate situation coming up with a witness that has asked for a closed session being one of the protective measures, and the Trial Chamber has agreed to that. So until the order is reversed, I'm afraid we will have to go into closed session. Thank you. Usher, please, could you prepare the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Just before --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before he's brought in, can I deal with two matters. First, the tapes. I'm assured that they will be ready before we break this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was an added extra message from Mr. Ackerman, but I'm not going to pass it on. The other matter is this: There was a Rule 92 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was a statement tendered under the provisions of Rule 92 bis which was accepted by Madam Fauveau and Your Honours, another member of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- family. Your Honour, the witness was 7.139. Can I ask that that be given the Exhibit number of 839.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 7.130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7.130, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 7.130. Your Honour, could I ask that it be marked a confidential exhibit because the details would disclose everything about the family and where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine there is no objection forthcoming from the Defence for having it filed --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please go ahead with tendering this document as Exhibit 7.1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, 839.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it will be admitted as confidential. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the next witness is in fact Charles McLeod. Your Honour, it may help Your Honour to know that this will be the fifth trial that he's testified in, so I don't think he needs much of an explanation beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact I had already decided not to explain anything to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm informed that you are quite familiar with the proceedings before this Tribunal, so we might as well proceed with the solemn declaration, which is contained -- the text of which is contained in that document. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down. You're going to be examined in chief by Ms. Korner for the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, is your full name Charles McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: My full name is Charles George Alexander McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, right. And Mr. McLeod, I want to ask you about the events in August of 1992 and later in October/November when you were a member of the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM. Before I do that, can I just ask you a little bit about your background. After leaving school, did you join the British army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you commissioned as a Second Lieutenant in September of 1982?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And thereafter did you serve as a platoon commander in Germany and later in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you then went to university and read German.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you rejoin your battalion full time in 1987?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you then in fact go to Northern Ireland for a two-year operational tour?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you then promoted to the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in fact, during this period, were you awarded the MB, the Member of the Order of the British Empire?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that you resigned your commission at the end of June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in July of that year, were you appointed to the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And during this period, did you undertake the activities in the area of North-West Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just -- because I think you're the first witness we've heard from ECMM. Can you tell us what the role of ECMM was in Bosnia at that period.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The fundamental operating procedure of the ECMM was to put two-man teams from different nationalities with an interpreter and a driver onto each side of a confrontation line wherever possible to try and start a dialogue between the military commanders on both sides of the contact line to enable them to stop fighting. And once that had taken place, then to try and establish confidence-building measures and then humanitarian actions. And the ECMM had been operating in Bosnia before I joined the mission but had left as the war had started. And when I was operating there in August 1992 we were attempting to re-establish a presence in Northern Bosnia, in the Serb-controlled part of Bosnia, as indeed we were also trying to re-establish a presence in the Croatian- and Muslim-controlled parts of Bosnia with a view to re-establishing our normal operations of understanding what was going on and trying to create a dialogue between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in respect of your activities and meetings that took place at the end of August and early September, did you keep notes of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And subsequently, did you turn those notes into a report for ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to look at a series of reports that you prepared of meetings, and I think you've brought with you the original notebook in which you made the notes on which you based your report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we start, please, with the report? Actually, before we do that, I think before you went to Banja Luka and met with the mayor and other people, were you given or sent a fax confirming that arrangements had been made for you to visit Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, first of all at a copy of the fax which was -- it's this one. I think I've actually got -- attachment 8 it was. We can see that at the top it comes from Banja Luka, and there's a phone number. And at the bottom, is that the official stamp showing the receipt of this fax?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated -- it's quite difficult to read, but I think it's the 19th of August, 1992, and it comes from somebody called R. Kosic, in Banja Luka, "Attention: Mr. T Michels." Who is Mr. Michels?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: He was an ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Subject: Visit to Banja Luka on August 20th, 1992," referring to your fax of the 18th. "Dear sir: "This is to confirm the subject visit as proposed. Only, the escort will be like follows: "Your team will be met at the Novska crossing and escorted from the point of Bosanska Gradiska by the police of Republic of Serbian Krajina. "At Bosanska Gradiska OLR Kosic will wait for you with a police guard at --" Is that "8 yards"? It's quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It's "800 hours."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "800 hours," right, "and escort you to Banja Luka. Stay at Banja Luka from 900 to 1500 hours as proposed. Turn trip the same," something, "as arrival," I think. "Expecting to meet you tomorrow. "Best regards - P. Radic, The Mayor." End of message. Right. Now can we move to the meeting that you had on the 20th of April? And I'd like you to look, please, at your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that fax be made Prosecutor's Exhibit P840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Exhibit number 840. Prosecution Exhibit P840.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could you be shown, please, the first of your reports dated the 23rd of August but referring to the meeting of the 20th of August, which is attach -- was attachment 1 to the statement. Mr. McLeod, how many of you had gone from ECMM to that meeting? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There were four of us, three people who'd been the previous team working in Northern Bosnia and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can see that it's dated the 23rd of August, and the subject is the Banja Luka recce, as it's described. And if we look at the introduction first of all: "The recce to Banja Luka was carried out by an ECMM team with the aim of beginning the process of re-establishing an ECMM presence in Banja Luka. The team had a meeting with Mr. Radic, the Mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Zupljanin, the Banja Luka Chief of Police, and Colonel Vukelic, a representative of the 1st Krajina Corps, followed by lunch." And it goes on: "I wrote detailed reports on much of what was said during the meeting, and this is a report based on those notes." And I think if we just read the general points, because I think it's repeated for each of your reports. "General points: The following general points should be kept in mind when reading this report: "a. I'm only reporting in the detail what was said by people we met, not on our sides of the conversations. "b. Although I wrote notes on large sections of discussions, there are gaps when I left the room to make phone calls, when the conversation broke down into general chat, and when specific names or places that I missed were mentioned and when I lost the flow. "c. This report should not be taken as a complete record of what was said. It is written with the aim of providing a feel for what concerned the men that we spoke to. And for that reason, I have included my explanation and comment throughout the text." Now, before looking at the -- and we may summarise a lot of this. Had any of your team met Mr. Radic before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. The other three members of the team had all met him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't know. I would assume that they had, but I don't know definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And Colonel Vukelic, the representative of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Again, I don't know whether they actually had, but it's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So as far as you were concerned, though, this was your first meeting with all three men?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you take along an interpreter or was an interpreter provided by Mr. Radic and his team?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: We had taken an interpreter with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we can see the conversations. At first where we see "Comment": "At first the only people present were Mr. Radic and his interpreter Mr. Kosic." So you both had interpreters, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if we summarised the first part, Mr. Radic was raising with you the Serbs being held, first of all, prisoner in a place called Rascani, and then effectively the Serb view or the world is not taking, as you put it, note of the Serbian suffering at Croat hands. Could we move to the next page, page 2. We see that your position under the headline -- second headline "Comment" was put outlining your aims and ending with a direct question about what freedom of movement could be offered by Mr. Radic in Banja Luka. And he told you that there was freedom of movement for international organisations, but again said this wasn't the case with some areas. And then if we see the sentence: "Here we have opened all our PW camps." Was that "prisoner of war camps"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he goes on: "Until your head of mission can give us reports on our prisoners of war, reports of people in the Green Beret's and Ustasha camps, we will not allow you total freedom here." Was this an issue that had been raised before or was this -- as far as you were aware, or was this the first time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: This was a new issue because previously we'd had teams working throughout Bosnia, and the main thrust of what Radic was saying was that until we could operate and report equally in each of the Serb-controlled, Croatian-controlled, and Muslim-controlled areas, then he'd seen no reason why we should be given complete freedom to operate in just his area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I think we can move on, then, because there was discussion then, it looks like, about whether there were teams -- that ECMM was going to other areas as well. If we go to the next page, please, to where Colonel Vukelic intervened, stating that "The position of our people and our nation is such that any aid is welcome, as is any international organisation that is here in goodwill and respects the sovereignty of our nation." And then he goes on to talk about organisations and institutions passing through our zone and states: "The effects are very small. I would not like to estimate why that was the case but most probably due to the fact that the conference is not finished yet and many already recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state." What conference was he referring to at that stage?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There was one of the many conferences being organised by the International Community to try and bring the parties together, and on that occasion there was a conference in London where they were trying to sort out a political solution for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he goes on to talk about 3.5 million Serbs and their interests being bypassed. Then he talks about what happened with delegations. "I was personally a witness of the state of many delegations from the UN to the ICRC. Many of them came with given tasks in advance. You can imagine if a group of journalists came to one camp and all of them address their attention to the person who looks bad and they do not pay attention to the healthy people. You must allow that some people are healthy and some are weak. It leads to a report that conditions are bad. Such behaviour brings greater reward for the journalists." And I think -- again, I'm going to move on quickly through this report. Colonel Vukelic had quite a lot to say. And if we go to the next page, page 4, we see at the -- near the bottom -- three paragraphs from the bottom, he said: "There are problems with the blockade in this area. The ICRC representatives requested that we improve the conditions of the prisoners of war, and today I am forced to ration only two meals for my soldiers. When the ICRC specify 2.800 calories for each prisoner of war and I could not provide --" as written "220." But I think you made a note. You thought that must have been an error.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know at that stage what prisoner of war camp he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that we were aware there were camps -- I think at that stage we weren't talking specifically about Manjaca or Trnopolje. I think -- I can't remember the exact detail, but there had been at about that time a photograph of a person standing against somewhere on the front page of, I think, Time. And I think he was probably referring back to that, but I can't -- I don't have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we just move on again, Mr. Radic talks about the refugees in the Bosanska Krajina and the lack of electricity and the like, and then exchanges of prisoners of war. Now, can we go over the page to the page 6, because that was the first time that Mr. Zupljanin spoke. And your note was that effectively, "He spoke at length. He had what looked like a prepared script in his notebook and seemed to paraphrase it." And his position was this: "Many things have changed since your departure and many more people are dead and many of us did not want this war." And he went on to say: "I think we are not prepared to make concessions to anyone because our impression is that the world does not want to hear the truth. It is easy to walk relatively safely in Bosanska Krajina thanks to us, but some places are not safe. Genocide is being committed there. We are blamed that prisoners of war are starved, our babies die without oxygen, and that is not recognised. Sarajevo gets aid but no one mentions Banja Luka and 176.000 refugees are here. Therefore prove your force, let us open the airport and then we shall trust in your abilities and goodwill; otherwise we will understand that you cannot help." He then talked about energy and the railway and then said this: "International intervention: We are not afraid of threats and will not give in. If intervention is used, it can only help the Serb nation and other nations here to get more comfort. These are the flames of the beginning of the Third World War and they will certainly get to the rest of Europe too. I regret that you may not like much of what I have said. I agree that we cannot agree on all issues ..." And then were you asked -- did you raise the question of freedom of movement for ECMM at the bottom of that page, and then Mr. Radic replied to that: "Escorts will be obligatory, not only on your request because there are regions and information that must be kept secret. That must be clear to you since this is the army opposed to two other armies and we would not want the other side to get such information. Therefore it is up to the military authorities. The escort must provide security and will take you to areas that the authorities say can be visited because of the sensitivity of interests or information." And then you added a comment: "They were asked if the sensitive areas stayed the same or changed, and the response was that they changed. The point was then made that if someone has something that is neither military nor sensitive to hide, they simply put it out of bounds." And Radic replied to that: "We guarantee we will not do that. We must have trust. It is obligatory." And then there's more discussion about entry to areas that -- for security reasons. There was lunch, and you at item 4 tried out an argument with Mr. Radic which didn't apparently get very far, and Colonel Vukelic also had his bit to say. "General impressions." Can we come to those. "Mr. Radic seemed pleased to see us. He started by taking the line that he was only the local man and not in a position to call the shots. In practice I think that he was calling some of the shots, although he deferred to both the police and the army." Now, can I ask you about that. I know it's difficult casting your mind back ten years or so, but what was the impression that he was seeking to give when you first spoke to him? I mean, by saying he was only the local man. Who was he saying was in a position to call the shots?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: He was saying that he was in control of the town, the area around the town. He was saying that above him there was a government structure and therefore he couldn't speak on behalf of the government but he could only talk about Banja Luka. And equally he was a civilian within a tripartite management of the civilian, military, and the police and there were obviously matters over which he was not in control because they were matters for the police or the military, I think would summarise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then under B, "Inspector Radic: Initially discussion our return, it seemed that the principle of putting teams on all sides within a few days was not negotiable. However, when talking about the time-scale for our next visit and future activities, I gained the impression that he accepted that we might be mounting missions on a daily basis by the end of next week without the need for teams elsewhere." And you noted that "He was well prepared for the meeting, with a folder containing notes and documents, a list of prisoner of war faxes from the ECMM, and a cartoon drawn by a monitor which he produced as an icebreaker." The list of prisoner of war faxes from ECMM, do you know to what that refers?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. I think I was saying that he had a list of prisoners of war and that he also had faxes from ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I'm sorry, yeah. I'm misreading. And then coffee and juice for everyone, except Colonel Vukelic, who didn't get any. "7. Mr. Zupljanin was trying to be friendly with both eye and physical contact, had what looked like a prepared script. I think that he was basically positive in his attitude through the double-talk. He made several references to the availability of girls and the prospects of nightlife for the team, and he told a joke about a policeman who shoots a man just before curfew because he knows where he lives and knows he'll not be able to get home in time (an old joke). "Colonel Vukelic had a degree of eye contact but it was more guarded. He was more passionate in his statements, detailing the lack of things in Bosanska Krajina and the difference between the treatment he was expected to give prisoners of war and could give his troops. He was very strong on credibility or the lack of it on our part. "9. Conclusions: I formed the impression that they were pleased to see us and that along with recognition, humanitarian aid for their prisoners of war, and the refugees and population as a whole is a top priority. They were quite hard on the principle of working on all sides, however I am not convinced this will be enforced. They made repeated references to the coming winter, and I believe they have a strategic desire to have international aid to get them through the winter without weakening their negotiating position." Again, Mr. McLeod, those are your conclusions. What impression did you get from these three men about their attitude towards your arrival or your coming back into the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, the impressions as opposed to report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can. If you can't really say anything beyond the report, then say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think the report probably summarises it. They were pleased to see us. They were keen that we should be providing recognition for their government and very interested to see whether we could provide them information on Serbs in other areas where they knew there were things going on but had no information. So that was -- that was fairly high on their agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move then, please, to the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that all these reports be made part of the same exhibit number, which will be 851 I -- sorry, 841. So if that report could be 841.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to these being made exhibits. And if that's going to be the case, then perhaps it won't be necessary for Ms. Korner to read them to us any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Ackerman, has just suggested it's been crossing your mind for quite some time during the first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're happy with living with what has been suggested by Mr. Ackerman and go direct to specific questions that you would like to ask the witness, then perhaps we could even finish with him quicker than -- than anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes. I mean, if it hadn't have been -- I might have taken -- but it seems to me this is one way -- I mean, it's the usual thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is one way. I mean, I'm not stopping you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in other words, you have a hint from the Defence that they are -- there is no objection forthcoming from their part as to the tendering of these documents as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I fully appreciate, Your Honour. I am fully aware that the Defence are -- would prefer the documents not be read out. Your Honour, I am going to summarise them as much as I can until I reach the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, Ms. Korner. It's up to you. You know what the priorities are as far as your witness is concerned, that he must return by a specific --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour has already ruled there's no cross-examination today, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you then to have your second -- hand your second report, please, for the meeting of the 25th of August, which is attachment 2. I'm sorry, the meeting was the 24th of August. Could you be handed it. This was the second visit on the 24th, so that was some four days later. Was it the same team, Mr. McLeod, as before? If you can remember.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember if all four of us were the same. Certainly three of the four of us were the same. I think one of the members of the team might have left by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And while we're just dealing with that, was one of the members of that team who came with you on these visits somebody called Barney Mayhew?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who had been in the area, as you pointed out, earlier?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This time it was Mr. Radic and a Mr. Bulic attended, representing the Banja Luka police. And I don't think on this occasion that there was anybody from the army who attended. In fact, I think you raised it with him, as we'll see. Can we just see how it started? "At first the only people present were Mr. Radic and his interpreter, Mr. Kosic. There were very brief greetings and then Mr. Radic made a strong opening attack," in which he said, you'll note: "Did you get permission from the Bosanska Krajina government to arrange this visit? And if not, why not?" What was his attitude like, that on the second meeting? At the beginning, in any event.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, the comment that I wrote suggested that he was being fairly forceful. I can't honestly remember the precise detail of the meeting, but if that was the impression that I formed at the time, then that's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he actually -- when he said, and you probably can't remember, but did he -- when he said, "Did you get permission from the Bosanska Krajina government," did he mention any names in particular, even if you can't remember the names now? If he had -- or if he had, would you have made a note?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think he said "government," and I think I then added -- in my note, I think I actually wrote "government." I can go back and check it. And I think I then added in "Bosanska Krajina" because that was what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So just summarising that, you were still discussing the question of the return of ECMM. And if we look at the second page, Mr. Radic -- you discussed the method of operating, and Mr. Radic said: "You will be able to visits those parts of the territory that are approved by the authorities and have an obligatory escort in areas covered by the war. Did you understand that?" And then he goes on to explain that you needed an escort in Banja Luka until the inhabitants, effectively, got used to you. Then Mr. Bulic arrived, and Mr. Radic went on discussing the prisoners of war camps and people that he had spoken to. And taking this much more shortly, I think you also gave him some information about - this is at page 6 - about the findings of the ECMM team that went to Tomislavgrad and Rascani on the 22nd of August. Those areas being what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Tomislavgrad and Rascani were areas within Croatian -- areas within Bosnia controlled by the Croats. And specifically in Rascani, there were a number of Serbs - it had been a Serb village, I think originally - who were being held by the Bosnian Croats, and, therefore, he was interested to know what their conditions were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we go over to page 7, please, where Mr. Radic was asked if there had been many examples of attacks in the Bosanska Krajina against Croats or Muslims, and his answer to that was: "Those were not individual acts but the war. Unfortunately, from all three sides there were incidents, ugly ones, but not from Banja Luka opstina." And then he gave some lists of how many people had been killed. And then -- and said: "All are under investigation by the police." And then he said. "When regular military forces are in question, they are in the strict control of their commanders, but there are also those who just put on the uniforms, procure somehow the arms, and they do not decide or differentiate who to mistreat. "We are arresting them, by the military and police, because by international convention, men wearing uniforms and carrying arms are treated as prisoners of war. In war it is easy to get both, but we will clean them out in Banja Luka and also in other cities." And you made a comment at the top of the following page that this struck you as a formula for not according prisoner of war status to any group of men whom it is more convenient to treat as criminals. And there was a mention of 16 Croat prisoners who he had talked about, and he said that they were well, and, as far as he knew, they were in Manjaca. And he said: "Of course you will have to discuss it with the military authorities because I'm not in charge of prisoner of war." And finally, again, then, moving to the end of this meeting, page 9. He made this comment: "Talking of Banja Luka, I would like to say that Banja Luka without Muslims and Croats is like wine without the bouquet. They all give characteristics to the city. If anyone is taken out it will not be the same city. We even have one part with Gypsies and would not want to lose them. "Unfortunately, they are not touched by anyone in this war. I was sad to hear in Kozarusa the Green Berets killed Gypsies who did not want to join them and liquidated them." And then at item 6, you said -- stated that you asked Mr. Kosic why the meeting had not been attend by the military and by a policeman who said nothing. "He said that they were waiting for the London conference to produce something and that they do not think anything will be settled until then." And then you made your -- you jotted down your general impressions on that, ending up by saying that -- well, effectively at the end, it was a low profile meeting from their point of view and that the information about Rascani caught them off guard, and they fully expect something to cool out of the London conference. All right. Now can we move to the next part. Is what then happened that the London conference or subsequent to the London conference there was a mission sent to Bosnia by the organisation the CSCE?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which was headed by Sir John Thomson?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the aim of that part of the mission, in any event, to visit the camps that had been said to be in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed in other areas as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as a result of that, were you sent to effectively facilitate the mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you then accompany Sir John Thomson and a number of other people, in fact, on that visit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then go next to the report that you made -- oh, yes. I'm sorry. Can I exhibit that report as 841.3 -- 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, I'm taking it that all the attachments from 1 to 7 will -- are being tendered as exhibits of the Prosecution from 841.1 to .7 respectively; correct? So you don't have to repeat it each time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you came into the area through Bosanska Gradiska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I think we're waiting for me to see the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I hadn't realised it hadn't been given to you. Could you be handed the report 1st of the 9th? You made a number of -- in fact, I think we might give you the whole collection on -- of -- there are one, two --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a little problem with the annexes because we don't have the numbers on the annexes. I would, nevertheless, like Madam Korner to state the number on each occasion, the number of the document concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next report that I'm going to ask you to be handed is dated the 1st of the 9th, 1992, and it is headed "Meeting With the Mayor of Bosanska Gradiska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The English version, and I suppose that's the one that you have as well, ERN number is 00950336. That's the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have that number either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Attachment number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Attachment number 3, yes. How come the attachment that they have doesn't have the official ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know Your Honour. I have no idea at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have just one number, 7.52, and above that the word "Attachment." The documents that we have don't have an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may well have been disclosed before it was stamped. These -- these were -- it almost certainly was, Your Honour. I think what happened was we had to get permission from ECMM to -- disclosed on the 3rd of May, 2000. Are you saying you don't have a copy, Madam Fauveau? Because if so, we will provide you with one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't understand her saying so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the documents, but it's difficult for us to find the relevant document. We can find it only on the basis of date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are two from the 1st of September, and if you look at the subject, it says: "Meeting With the Mayor of Bosanska Gradiska." Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can deal with this one very briefly. You met with Mr. Ivastanin Nebojsa - I don't think that's a very good pronunciation - the mayor, and I think he was complaining about the attacks from Croatia. And if we look at paragraph 14, he was complaining about the genocide in World War II and so on and so forth. And I don't, in fact, think we need to go through that. However, did he show you -- could you look at page 4 of your report, Mr. McLeod? Did he show you what was described as shell damage from the night before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there was an unoccupied storage facility which had a 3.5 diameter -- 3.5 metre diameter hole in it claimed being caused by a rocket. I want to ask you this: You said "claimed." I mean, with your military experience did you accept that or not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There was certainly a hole in the roof. I hadn't seen the effects of a rocket on a roof, so I wasn't sure whether that was the sort of damage that you would expect to get, but there was certainly not a great deal of damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you would -- "While looking at the building, we were told that the population was now 63 per cent Serb and 25 per cent Muslim. Also told that there had been some individuals who had left the town as refugees but no group." Then can we look at your general impressions? The first comment about this meeting was: "The high level of security that had been laid on, with piquets every 100 metres and the desire to make it seem important. "The second was the very direct manner in which Mr. ***," that's presumably the Mayor, "introduced the subject of cantonisation and discussed Croat acceptance of the principle. "The attempt at drawing sympathy for their suffering as a result of the shelling failed entirely because this building they chose was away from the populated areas and was not convincing. "Conclusion: This meeting had been carefully orchestrated and set out by the basic position of the Serb authorities. Most of the points raised were reinforced by the subsequent meeting with Mr. Radic." And I think we'll look at that before we come back to the impression. So could you have a look, please, at the next report from that date, the meeting with the mayor of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau, if you have difficulty in locating this document, it's again dated the 1st of September of 1992, and the subject is: "Meeting with the Mayor of Banja Luka." Okay. Thank you. Are you having problems, Mr. Ackerman, with your documentation or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have the same problem Ms. Fauveau does, but I'm finding the documents and getting them marked. They don't have any indications on them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I just wanted to make sure. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So did you -- you moved down from Gradiska to Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And back to see Mr. Radic. And just so we get the chronology, you then went to Manjaca, the camp, and the following day did you go to Prijedor and then to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then here you see Sir John. It's written, so just correct -- it's item number 3, the conversations, comment of the introduction "Sir John Thomas." That should be "Thomson," should it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct. There are a number of typos in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was discussion, and I think we don't need to go through that there was discussion about the camps, about possible aid. And I'll just check. Yes. I'm sorry. Can we just go to paragraph 24 for a moment, please. There's a comment before that: "The conversation broke down into an explanation of the mission and the fact that it was looking at all camps." And Radic said: "On the territory of Bosanska Krajina, there is only one prisoner of war camp, the one that you will see today as Manjaca. The other one is not a prisoner of war camp. It is half open and cannot be classified as a prisoner of war camp. You will see it tomorrow." "At --" should that be Doboj?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I should think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "-- Doboj there is nothing. There are no other camps. Bihac, of course, is part of the Krajina but it is in the hands of the Muslims." Then Radic was asked if he thought it was possible or desirable to have mixed inspection teams for the camps. And he said he couldn't answer that; it would have to go across to Mr. Popovic. Do you remember what Mr. Popovic was? You don't seem to mention --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think he may have been a gentleman from the Ministry of Health, or that's what I got as my -- that was my impression. Yeah. I think he was the gentleman in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the -- your -- Sir John Thomson's team was accompanied by somebody from Pale, Mr. Popovic, who was from the Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's how he was introduced, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at the end of that meeting, did you and Sir John go to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'd like you to have a look at your report, please, on Manjaca. I'm sorry. Before we move to that, you said when you were completing your report on Gradiska about the mayor of Gradiska, that "The meeting had been carefully orchestrated and set out the basic position of the Serb authorities. Most of the points were reinforced by the subsequent meeting with Mr. Radic." Can you just explain what you mean by the meeting being carefully orchestrated.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The fact that the -- the route which we took from the bridge where you cross over into Bosanska Gradiska to the building in which the meeting took place was lined by -- oh, I can't remember whether they were soldiers or policemen, but men in uniform, anyway, all the way around, and the fact that we were escorted and shown various things. Obviously some thought had gone into this. It wasn't anything that hadn't been expected or for which no preparation had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the meeting with Mr. Radic - obviously this was your third or fourth meeting with Mr. Radic, I think, by then - but was the same -- was there the same feel about that, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I honestly can't remember, other than the notes that I have made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now can we come to, please, the visit to Manjaca itself. Can you have your report, please, which is headed "Meeting with the commandant of the PW camp Manjaca" dated the 3rd of September, referring back to the visit on the 30th. You see in paragraph 2 this report on the meeting with Colonel Popovic, the commandant of the prisoner of war camp at Manjaca, is based on these notes. Now, did Colonel Popovic meet you at the entrance to the camp, or were you taken to his office? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that he or certainly his officers met us outside and then took us through into the -- the administration area, into a conference room, I suppose is how you would describe it on the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he opened the conversation -- you say you made full notes. "Welcome to this prisoner of war camp." Gave his name, said he was the commandant. "I want to stress that this is a prisoner of war camp and not a concentration camp. I would like to apologise in advance for referring to some of the articles of the Geneva Convention with the wish in order to convince you that this camp is administered and functions and is run in accord with the Geneva Conventions." And then he went on to tell you that "There are around 3.640 prisoners of war. According to article 2, paras 79 and 80 of the Geneva Conventions have chosen themselves their representatives and deputy representatives and we hope and think that these people will always stick to the Geneva Conventions." "The people in the camp have been caught in the zone of combat." And he gave the article. "I responsibly state that we treat them very humanely and correctly in accordance with paragraphs -- as far as personal property is concerned, this is covered by article 18. Conditions of stay, used all the possibilities at our disposal to the effect of satisfying part 2. You will see yourselves here. You will see yourselves here. I would have been happier if I had hotels to put them in, but I have no such possibilities." One of the unfortunate things is hygiene and medical cover. And then he refers to the articles and the embargo. Now, before we go on, was he literally going through it, as you've recorded it, from what you remember?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that he had -- I think in one of my notes I comment -- I think he had a prepared script and so he had obviously noted out the relevant articles of the Geneva Conventions and was at great pains to stress to us that on the one hand he knew what the relevant things were and on the other hand he was complying with them as far as he possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he dealt with the -- he was asked about the embargo and you said the blockade against Yugoslavia. And you then made the comment -- or somebody made the comment that "The point was made that medicines are not embargoed." And then he said: "No medical aid because planes could not land. Tried everything in the spirit of articles 32 and 33 to ensure medical supplies for the sick," and then talked about washing and the ICRC. "Freedom of religion. Anyone who wants to practice religion -- but we haven't had a single request. We have sacked five religious employees. The representatives of --" I think that must be Merhamet or Mohammed it could be, I suppose "-- and the Catholics have taken them away." One of the activities of the headquarters is to make prisoners of war work. I wish to assure you we stick to article 50 of the Geneva Convention and use them only for the type of work that is foreseen by the Geneva Conventions. We had problems that everyone wanted to work, but we do not have that much work. Conditions of work. Communications with the outside world. They were abiding by article 73. And about 250 parcels have arrived for individuals. And then paragraph 15: "I would appreciate it if you pay particular attention to one thing. We have had six deaths. All occurred from natural causes. I mention it on purpose because I would like you to go to the other side and see what happened to 6.000 Serbs who disappeared on the other side. This is a list of camps where Serbs are imprisoned." At that stage can you remember was he handing over a list?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember. He may well have given John Thomson a list. I certainly don't have a copy of a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he said he kept a record of the workers according to the Geneva Conventions. He said there were six doctors and three medical technicians amongst the prisoners, that 25 prisoners had been taken care of in Banja Luka hospital, a good infirmary. Little or no medicines. And then the nationality: 125 Croats, 3.4 per cent; Serbs, 0.04 per cent; and Muslims, 96.5. And then the colonel was asked about Davor Glasnovic, a Canadian who was believed to have been in the camp, and that you were told he was in Banja Luka. And I think you made a comment that you tried to see him in the interrogation centre the following morning -- this is back in Banja Luka, is it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "We got as far as Mr. Radic's office but were told the investigating magistrate had decided that because Mr. Glasnovic's investigation was in progress, he could not be seen. And we were told that it might be possible in a week or so." And then he asked you to be truthful and objective and to inform public opinion. Then he went on to say -- I mean, there was Serb -- there was complaint about the exchanges with Mr. Izetbegovic and the like -- that 390 -- over 390 people had been freed, over 60 or under 18. Dealt with the humanitarian organisations, the media and other people who had visited. A group of Lords here from the UK, the ICRC. And then we look at the comment just before paragraph 33: "The commandant was asked how the prisoners of war were actually taken, if they were actually fighting or carrying weapons." And his reply was this: "There is the interrogation period. Everyone is being interrogated. And if it is proven that he did not take part in the fighting, he will be freed." So in fact that was the only answer you got to that question, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then he was asked about those who were unable to work because there was not enough work. And he explained the strict order of activities. "Groups allowed out to rest or work outside an average of four hours a day outside the blocks." And then he went on to say: "The Geneva Conventions say they should have two hours. This does not include the time when they go to the WC or queue for food or medicals and so on. I'm very sorry it is raining because you will not see them sitting in the sun." And then the point was made that was a minimum acceptable level and that standards should rise above it. He was asked about the letters and the camp -- he was then asked when the camp was formed and under whose control it was. "It was created in September, about the 15th, for a group of Ustasha, until the 1st of November, 1991. Then it was closed and not reopened until the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 15th of May, 1992. It is under the control of the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading for interpretation..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner, I've just received a complaint --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, the interpreter asked me before to slow down, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will. That's the difficulty with summarising.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then we move to questions about nutrition and the ICRC and if there were any restrictions on the prisoners of war visiting latrines. And you said there were twice a day, depending on their representatives during the day. And then he said: "In the morning I have to limit the time because of those who go to work." And then he explained at paragraph 42 this: "I have been a soldier since the age of 15. I was never really an orthodox soldier and my weak side is that I am a humanist and I do not allow any reprisals and repressions. Even children in the family need correcting. I respect only work, order, and discipline. " He was asked if there had been any escapes, and he said: "Not even one attempt. And as long as I am the commandant, no one will." He was asked when the camp will be closed, and the reply was: "It depends on the government." And at this stage Mr. Popovic, the health ministry man, interrupted and said: "We know the results of the London conference, and in this moment I am ready to sign on behalf of the Serb government an order to close all camps." And there was then further remarks by him. And then Colonel Popovic stated: "I was an officer in the JNA, and no one has the right to throw me out of Bosnia because I was born here and who can stop me defending my home." And then he talked about the Croatian regular army, prisoners of war in Banja Luka interrogation centre, one was a friend. And then the Canadian -- and apparently an American was exchanged. And then he was asked if the interrogation centre could be visited. If we then go to your general impressions. And this is where -- Colonel Popovic was speaking from a prepared script and quoted the Geneva Conventions by rote. "He was very sensitive on the subject of what he did with prisoners who stepped out of line, refusing to give any more explanation than that they were dealt with in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." I'm going to move next, Mr. McLeod, to your impressions of the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- perhaps that might be -- I think that's going to take a little bit more time, so it may be a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Mr. McLeod, we are going to break now for lunch. We will resume at 2.30, as planned yesterday. 2.30. And we'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it Court II at 2.30, Your Honour? I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Court II, as we were told?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to move to Court II. Yes, that is what we agreed yesterday. We will be moving to Courtroom number II at 2.30, and we will hope to finish --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will finish by 4.00 at the very latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm just standing up in anticipation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. You may wait one moment. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we won't have any problems later, could you just make a very brief oral order that the tapes which we've now received be transported with the detainees back to the detention centre because the -- I think security wants an order from the Court before they do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, the Chamber has taken note of the request put forward by counsel for Brdjanin. The Chamber accedes to the request and so orders accordingly. The copy of this part of the transcript is to be handed to the commandant or whoever is responsible for the Detention Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANVOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just like to make sure that this order is also applicable to General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The same order is being made applicable to General Talic. It was taken for granted, Madam Fauveau, because you do have a spare copy of these tapes as well, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Korner, you may proceed with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, just before the adjournment, we had dealt with your notes of the conversation, if that's the correct word, with Colonel Popovic. I'd now like you to describe to us, if you could, your impressions of what you saw in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. So the camp was based in what had obviously once been a farm on what was a military training ground, and the camp consisted of the farm administration buildings and then a number of what I assume were cattle sheds, and the cattle sheds were on the side of a sloping hill in two groups of three, and the area with the sheds was surrounded by a tall wire fence and then subdivided into two compounds of three sheds each, and there were armed men on the outside of the camp and controlling the front entrance. There was at least one watchtower with armed soldiers standing in it. Down at the bottom of the slope inside the wire there were two open-sided barns which were being used for preparing and eating meals by the detainees. Access, once you were inside the wire, to each of the compounds and then into the sheds themselves was being controlled actually by inmates. So they themselves were controlling access through the internal doors. Inside each of the sheds there was a door which opened at each end. Inside the shed there was a raised concrete platform down the middle of the shed; therefore, with two gullies, one on each side. When we went into each of the sheds, we found that they were full of men sitting in rows shoulder to shoulder, in six rows, so therefore packed into each building. As we went into each building, the men all stood up. It was apparent that there was a leader or a foreman inside each of the sheds who then addressed the commandant, and once the greetings, the interchange, had been made, the men were all told to sit down again. The men were sitting on blankets. They each had a blanket. They had their shoes off in front of them. And it was a bit like sardines in a tin is one way of describing it. Very, very closely packed. There was a medical facility -- I suppose a ward, you would call it, which looked again like a smaller cow shed, and there were a number of people lying on - I can't remember exactly what it was - but lying not on beds, and they had various injuries, mostly leg injuries. There was at least one person who had had a leg amputated; otherwise, broken legs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The prisoners themselves, were you able to speak to them at all?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. When we first went in, we asked if we could speak to them. We were told that we would be able to converse with a nominated person within each of the buildings, and a person was found. And that conversation was being connected through an interpreter, obviously with a lot of people standing around watching. I -- I speak fairly good German, and therefore I walked down the -- between the men and was trying to find somebody who could speak German - typically quite a lot of people in the former Yugoslavia can speak German - and was able to have a brief conversation with a couple of people. As soon as -- as soon as you struck up a conversation, then one of the guards walked down to listen in to see what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The people to whom you managed to talk, what was the conversation about roughly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: For --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps -- can I rephrase that. Did any of the people to whom you talked complain to you about their treatment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think I've characterised the conversations within my notes. It would be quite useful if I could then refer to those --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: -- if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you would like to, with Your Honours' permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. The witness may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my notes, I noted that there were basically five points which were made out of the conversations. The first question was do you know when we're going to be able to get out of here? That was the most pressing thing. The second point that was made was that there were no soldiers within the camp as prisoners. They said that the soldiers had already been shot previously. They said that conditions had improved significantly since the ICRC had started visiting and providing facilities. They said that they had been in this camp for about a month and that conditions were far worse in the previous place that they had been. I didn't establish exactly where they had been, but they had been in another facility for a couple of months before being moved to Manjaca. And they said there were lots of things which it simply was not safe to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, they told you that there were no soldiers here. Did you see anybody in uniform? That is, amongst the prisoners. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. There may have been a few people wearing bits of uniforms, but the overwhelming impression was that these were men wearing civilian clothes. And we asked why this was, and one of the people accompanying us, one of the Serbs accompanying us explained that they had needed the uniforms and therefore they had taken the uniforms off the men who were now being detained and had given them civilian clothes instead. I -- I found that hard to believe because the people seemed to be wearing clothes that fitted them as if they were their own clothes, so I think by and large they were actually wearing the clothes they had been wearing when they were picked up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that the prisoners were -- seemed to be packed like sardines in these barns that you visited. Did anything strike you about the position in which they were? They were sitting, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: If one had to sit on a concrete floor for 20 hours a day - say, if they're taking four hours out for work - that would be an excruciatingly uncomfortable thing to have to do, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you see the prisoners being taken for a meal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. As we were leaving, detainees were being taken in groups. They would be called up again by a member of the detainee community, and they would walk in rows with their heads bowed and their hands behind their heads in silence from the barns where they sat down to the - I can't think of a -- of a good way of describing it - the place where they were given their food.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You had been told by the colonel before you inspected that this was not a concentration camp. What was your view of the camp?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that it would be fair to say that based on this visit and some of the subsequent visits that I made -- or the subsequent visit that I made, that this was a camp in which a large number -- three and a half thousand male members of the predominantly Muslim population had been brought together to hold them until a solution was found for what to do next with them. I think that the majority of them probably had not been soldiers. There may well have been some fighting going on at the point when they were detained, but these were not soldiers. These were civilians who had been gathered together and they were being held and, therefore, not prisoners of war. And if a concentration camp is somewhere where you concentrate people into one place and indeed concentrate them very densely in one place, then this certainly was a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us about the conversations you were able to have with the prisoners. When the guards came and stood near you, did that seem to have an effect on the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. Very clearly they were not comfortable continuing to have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you were asked - and we'll have a look at a moment at a note you made after your second visit to Prijedor and Trnopolje - to give the Court your impressions of that camp when you left. Now, you've told us about -- what impression did that leave on you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I found it deeply disturbing. I had been inside a military prison while I was serving in the British army. I knew that the regime there was very hard, but certainly nothing like that which I was seeing here. And again, I recognise that people can have differences of opinion about who should be controlling which bits of territory. Back at home in Scotland there is a degree of antipathy towards the English because of historic differences. But to see people held under those conditions was frankly wrong and very upsetting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. When you left Manjaca, did you the following day in fact go to the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you now, please, to look at your report that deals with the visit you made, first of all, to Prijedor, in fact, in the -- when you met the mayor. That was number -- Attachment 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7 -- Attachment -- forgive me, Your Honour. I've just realised that I've missed out a -- a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, another report on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. There was another report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Manjaca, Dobrnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. And it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just have a look, please, at the report that you've dealt with on Manjaca. It's headed "Manjaca PW camp," dated the 3rd of the 9th, 1992. And I think you've really covered all the aspects of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for record purposes, when we refer to these reports, it might be helpful to -- to refer to the exhibit number so that we'll know what we're talking about when we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. For the record, we're talking about Exhibit -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 841.6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm sorry, and it's my fault. Can we just look for a moment at paragraph 16 of that report, Mr. McLeod, of the reaction of the authorities: "The Commandant, Colonel Popovic, was very clear that he wanted us to see everything and report accurately. However, we were not allowed to see everything and some questions were ignored. He quoted the Geneva Convention to justify all his actions. A separate report is being written on his interpretation of the Geneva Convention." Just this: What were you not allowed to see? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that we asked whether we could go and see some of the other buildings within the farm compound, and that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I don't know at this juncture, ten years on, can you remember what questions were ignored? Or was that just the questions we can see in your report that there wasn't an answer to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't think of anything beyond the points that I've made in the report at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. That then -- can we move then to your meeting with the mayor of Prijedor on the 3rd of September? I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. It was the 31st of August where you met with Dr. Stakic. And he gave you a sort of talk, it appears, explaining that the Muslim party had won the election, were in power for one and a half years, and took the opportunity it gave them to arm the most extreme parts of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Same thing. Can we can identify the Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We're referring to Prosecution Exhibit P841.7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And took the opportunity -- yes. I've dealt with that. "The preparation has reached a culminating point at the end of April, beginning of May, when these armed groups put up barricades and started shameful murders of the army of Bosanska Krajina and the police." Gave you a version of what had happened in Prijedor, said to you that: "In the homes of religious leaders we found US shotguns which in the US are forbidden for hunting." "Fighting and destruction," and, "Several people were captured." Paragraph 9: "There was fighting and destruction especially, in --" should that be Kozarac? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't know. We could look at a map and try and identify it, but that's the way it ended up in the note.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "...and several people were captured. We called on them to -- we called them to free the women and children and let them go. They put the women and children in the front lines and followed with their weapons. The police and army accepted these women and children and put them in buses and took them to safe havens." And then: "In the course of the next few days, the army and the police captured several thousand people and put them into Trnopolje to protect them from the fighting with the extremists. That was how it started as a collection centre." And then he talked about the help of the ICRC, having Muslims and Croats in the camp who wish to remain, about around 10.000. And then contacts with UNHCR. And then he mentioned at paragraph 15: "...Omarska, where people were caught with weapons, where 45 investigators interrogated and imprisoned people. And as a result, 1.300 were transferred to the camp at Manjaca and others either freed or transferred to the open camp exclusively because their homes had been destroyed, so they have to go somewhere." And then there was the help of the Red Cross, welcome to the delegation, and so on and so forth. Then he was asked apparently what help he wanted, and he dealt with medicines and food and the London conference. And at paragraph 21 stated: "Neither Croatian nor Muslims left this territory, nor do we have the intention of kicking them out. There are some who hold appointments in the town and some in the forces." And then there was talk about the electricity and somebody called Mr. Kovacevic [sic]. So Mr. -- I don't -- you didn't, I don't think, listed, did you, the people, the names of the people who were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But there was clearly somebody called Mr. Kovacevic [sic]?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or "Kovacic" I suppose it's spelt. And there was more about the electricity, the corridors. And then if we go to paragraph 28, Dr. Stakic was asserting that: "There was equal treatment for all. Some Muslim areas have not been touched by war. We support your ideas for negotiations." And then, "Mr." blank, "member of the regional government." Is that somebody whose name you clearly didn't get at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't imagine you can remember, but by regional government, do you mean the government in Prijedor or something higher than that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I was -- I was noting the fact that he was introduced as somebody from the regional government without being able to find out further actually where he sat within a hierarchy [Realtime transcript read in error "higher ark i"].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right and he addressed you on the problem of, effectively, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I don't think we need trouble in this case to go through that. And then there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Line 11:1, the word shut be "hierarchy," h-i-e-r-a-r-c-h-y, not "higher ark i."
