utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then there was talk about exchange of prisoners, and you were going to be shown some Muslim currency but there was no electricity at that stage. And then if we go over, please, to page 5, paragraph 36, "Mr. ?." So was this the man who had been introduced as a member of the regional government? Or could it have been somebody else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It would have been anybody. At this stage, I simply don't remember who was -- who was making the different points.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stated: "We have released a certain number of prisoners from the camp who were from here and who are still around, but in proposing an exchange, we take a risk because we know as soon as they go back they will be mobilised and fight against us. We have already had experience of this." And then Dr. Stakic said that: "Kozarac is still not yet a safe place because the extremists still come back and shoot, and yesterday we had two casualties and they were killed." And then there's talk about Mount Kozara and then reference to Hitler and the four years that he couldn't get rid of the fighters. 38: "When we insist on not calling it a camp, it is because the Serbs from here know very well what a concentration camp is, particularly on the other side." And then there was -- exchange was raised again. And finally your general impression: "The version of events that led to the opening of Trnopolje that we were given by the mayor was in stark contrast to that given by the people that we spoke to in the camp." So can I take it from that that you'd been to Trnopolje before you saw the mayor of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. But I wrote the report after I had been both to have the meeting with the mayor and then subsequently been to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. "Conclusion: The authorities insist that they are acting in the best interests of all the people in their area and that they have no desire to get rid of the Muslim population. However, this does -- this just does not match what they are actually doing. Against this background, it is very hard to draw conclusions based on what is said." 43: "The conclusion to be drawn from what we have seen is that the Muslim population is not wanted and is being systematically kicked out by whatever method is available." Now, you wrote this report after you'd been to Trnopolje and after you'd been to Manjaca and the other places. What was it that you saw that led you to the conclusion that the Muslim population was being systematically kicked out by whatever method is available?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The -- in very simple terms, the theme that ran through what a number of people had said to us was that at a certain point in time, the Muslim population had been rounded up, the women and children had been separated from the men, they had been put into different camps, and already by then we had seen large numbers of Muslims being bused from Northern Bosnia out into Croatia. And everything that one could see happening then and indeed later on pointed to the fact that there was one section of the community that was not wanted by another section of the community, and they were being removed fairly forcibly. And in turn, just to characterise something which was common across all parts of the former Yugoslavia, their homes were being destroyed to make it quite clear that they should not then come back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I deal then with the visit that you made to Trnopolje? I think your view is you must have written a report. For whatever reason, we haven't acquired that, but I think this is right: that you wrote to your father giving your impressions of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like -- I think -- I'd like you to have just the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've extracted. The rest of the letter is irrelevant. So this is just an extract from the letter that deals with his impressions. Could you be handed, please, just the extract. And that, Your Honour, will become whatever it is. The next -- 8 -- .8. Sorry. Could we make that .8 of the same exhibit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Reminding -- using that, refresh your memory, Mr. McLeod, what was your impressions of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: So this appeared to be the site of a former school, and the camp was bounded on two sides by a road. At the apex of the two roads there was a machine-gun covering down the two roads, pointing inwards to cover down the two roads. The camp was called an open reception centre. There was a sign which clearly said that it was an open reception centre. There were no fences around the outside of the camp. There were a large number of mostly men. I don't know exactly how many were there. We were guessing or people were saying between 1.600 and 4.000 people living in plastic shelters that were very makeshift. Here we were able to move amongst the men and they came and talked to us, as opposed to Manjaca, which was an extremely regimented environment. But the story that was being told again was -- was almost exactly the same. People were saying, "How long are we going to be here? We want to get out. And we're being kept alive by the fact that the ICRC is now providing us with food."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were told -- you'd been told by Mayor Stakic and others that this is somewhere people were going because their houses had been burnt and that it was a reception centre. Given that you say there was a machine - I'm sorry. Let me get the right - a machine-gun covering two roads down inwards, was that of any particular relevance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The -- the Serb military or police arm who were controlling the camp -- who were around the camp explained to us that this was there for the protection of the people who were living in the camp, to make sure that nobody came in from the outside and beat them up. It's quite clear that there were -- there were no fences around the outside, so people could come and go as they wanted to. However, I think that again it was pretty apparent when you were there that people were there because they had been told to be there and were not being encouraged to wander off home, if you want to put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, on the drive to and from Trnopolje, did you notice anything about the conditions of houses along the road?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly some -- some of the houses were obviously still occupied and people were living in them. Other houses were destroyed variously, mostly by being burnt. And again a -- a not untypical scene at that time in the former Yugoslavia, but the houses would have been burnt so that the roofs collapsed and you had the walls standing but the roofs collapsed. And they would typically indicate that there hadn't been heavy fighting in the area, just that the houses had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you take a series of photographs or a number of photographs during the course of this trip?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I took -- I took a number of photographs. In general, photography was forbidden. However, as I was leaving at the end of the day that we had been to Trnopolje, I took a number of photographs of the houses as we were driving out on the road from Prijedor back to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you to look, please -- in fact, I'm going to deal with all the photographs together, although one was taken earlier and one was taken later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before you proceed with showing the photos to the witness. The extract from -- his letter to his father. That's going to be P841.8 [Realtime transcript read in error "P814.8"]?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I wonder if the witness could have them. There are copies available for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are - one, two, three - six -- seven. I'd ask they be exhibited as 842.1 to 7, Your Honour. I'm going to ask that they be put up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, for the record, I didn't say that's going to be P814.8. I said it's going to be P841.8. And that's with reference to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The previous document, yes. Your Honour, can I go through them. And I'll show the numbering as we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first photograph, so that will be P842.1. Mr. McLeod, is it -- it's clearly not you, but is that an ECMM monitor in the white and the cap?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. That was a gentleman called Mark Vogola [phoen], who was a monitor from the Netherlands in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And is this right, it shows the -- near Karlovac, I think. It's the crossing-over from Bosnia to Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. This is in the village of Turanj, which was near Karlovac and was the crossing point -- the boundary point between the Serb and -- Serb-controlled part of Croatia and the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that taken in fact on the 23rd of July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then could we look at the next photograph, which we numbered .2. Is -- I'm sorry. Is that the right order? Is that the one that you numbered 2? I think you've got the originals there, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the one you numbered 2, is it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that shows what? If you could tell us, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: This and the subsequent photographs are houses on the north side of the road between Prijedor and Banja Luka in the Kozarac area, which I took on the 31st of August when I was driving back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's .2. If we could look at the next one. As you say, the same route, same road. Could I -- I'm sorry, can we just go back for one moment to the last photograph. The house that was still standing next to the two that have been burnt out, from your experience and from talking to people in the area, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's probably a house which was occupied by a Serb and so was continuing to live there, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So that was -- we've done the third. Can we now go to the fourth photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have the dates that these -- we have the date that the first one was taken. Are they all taken on July 23rd?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The 31st of August, coming back from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: August?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first photograph was July. He said the remainder were taken on the drive back from Trnopolje on the 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we look at 7199 again. It's actually 842.3. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Could we look at photograph number 4 next. And you just say the same thing. Number 5, and number 6. And then the final photograph, number 7, Mr. McLeod, I think that was taken in October -- the 1st of October, 1992, and shows us what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: So these are people who had been taken by the ICRC from Trnopolje and they were being taken from the Serb-controlled part of the UNPA across to the Croatian side, and they had been moved up to the contact line in Serbian buses. And obviously the Serbian buses couldn't then cross over into Croatia, so the men all had to get off the buses and walk down through no man's land. And that was a fairly hairy experience, with minors on both sides of the road in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you. That concludes the photographs. Now, Mr. McLeod, I think in the evening of the 31st of August, after you'd been to Manjaca and Trnopolje, did you make a note of your feelings in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if you could follow in your original, because we have a typed version and I want to check if there are any mistakes. Did you record this at 6.00 in the evening: "Driving from Prijedor to Banja Luka in the murk --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Korner, which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Your Honours should have a typed document, which is -- it's -- the -- I don't know if you were given the original. Yes, it says "Charles McLeod - personal notes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Starting with --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's the very last entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated the 31st of August, 1992 and it's 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And are you going to tender this as a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that would be P843?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. As -- we'll tender both the photocopy of the original and the typed version as -- perhaps as A and B. So the original will be A and the typed version B -- oh, there's a B/C/S, is there, as well? Okay, C then. I don't know if we need a B/C/S version exhibited, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is what you recorded: "Driving from Prijedor to Banja Luka in the murk. Now fixed. Under one-man police escort, lights flashing, ramming people off the road in front. I need to write but don't know what to say or where to start. I'm letting myself think just a little about what I have seen over the last couple of days and learnt, and I want to throw up or cry. Throwing up might be due to the 12-hour-old sandwich I have eaten, but the tears are emotion. The images are of the rows of men sitting on blankets in cattle sheds looking but not talking and standing eating at a bench in an open barn, then falling in a squat."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There's actually a discrepancy there. What I wrote was: "Then falling in as a squad."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "As a squad."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: "Heads bowed, hands behind their backs, to be shuffled back to their sheds by one of their own."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I wonder -- in that case, Mr. McLeod, it's probably better if you can read from your original from here on in and we'll just follow in the typed version. From the words "I spoke to two men there."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: "I spoke to two men there in German, both of whom were afraid to talk or tell me the truth but told me that much. They had been moved there a month ago and that was a luxury compared with the last place."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you pause, please. "That was a luxury."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Indeed. "That was a luxury."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: "They said there were no soldiers. They had all been shot. They were certainly wearing civilian clothes and someone on the escort team told me it was because they needed their uniforms so had taken them and replaced them with civvies."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can you just pause there. "They said there were no soldiers. They had all been shot. They were certainly wearing civilian clothes..."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, from the words "I am thin."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: "I am thin but so are all of them. There was a spark in some eyes, but many were deadpan. When we left and drove back past the dining sheds, they all waved at us as we waved through the armoured glass. Sick. I want to write the name of a well-known rugby club," which was of course is the Barbarians. "Today we drove to Prijedor. And on the road in most of the houses had been burnt but not to the ground. Then we had a meeting with the mayor."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what you wrote then, Mr. McLeod. Do you still feel the same way about what you saw that day and the previous day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally this: Some months later -- well, in fact did you deal, as we've seen from the photographs, with the -- or help out with the transfer of the people in Trnopolje from Trnopolje to Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in November of 1992, did you go back to Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that to assist the International Red Cross as they transferred prisoners who had been released from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got to Manjaca, where were the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The detainees who were going to be released were all standing outside the front of the camp in rows on the road waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the weather like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was bitterly cold, and I think it was snowing. It was certainly freezing cold.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you remember what sort of clothing they had?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think they were basically wearing the same clothes they'd been wearing the last time we'd been there in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else that struck you about that, that day when they were released? Did anybody make any speeches that day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. Once the whole thing was -- was ready to go, the -- oh, I suppose the -- the detainee leaders, the prisoners' leaders, whoever they were, asked whether they could address the commandant, and he said yes, they could. And they made a number of speeches saying how grateful they were for the excellent treatment which they had had whilst in Manjaca and thanking him for being the commandant. And then they got onto the buses and we drove off to Banja Luka and then up to Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When this -- these speeches were being made, clearly you were present. Were also representatives of the International Red Cross present at the same time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. They had to go through a process of interviewing each of the men before they were released to make sure they wanted to be released. That's one of the processes that the ICRC have to go through under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were any journalists there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I -- I don't think there were. I'm not sure, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, Mr. McLeod, just to complete this. I think you also assisted the International Red Cross in the release of Serb detainees who were being held in Bihac by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. So we -- we accompanied the ICRC from the detention centres - I think there were a couple of them within the Bihac pocket - out through Karlovac, all the way through Croatia, and then took them to Belgrade, where we handed them over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And equally it's right, I think, that you've never met either of the accused; that is, General Talic or Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner, it has been suggested to me that the -- Yes. Mr. Ackerman, let me finish this first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that the original of Mr. McLeod's so-called notes will be P843, and then the version -- the English version, typed version, and the other typed version, B/C/S, will be P843.1 and .2. Is that okay for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Madam Registrar... Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- there was one page, page 58 of Exhibit P -- what is now P843.1 that was actually read out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and compared with his original notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On that page, there are six errors. It's a 60-page document. If you multiply that times six, there's a presumption, at least, that there are 360 errors in these typed-up version of the notes. I think that is too error-filled to be permitted into evidence, and I'd therefore object to it being put into evidence in its current condition. It can be fixed, and I think it probably should be fixed, because some of these errors actually change the -- the meaning of some of these sentences. And I don't know how to deal with that. I don't -- I don't mind having it in evidence if it's accurate, but I think it should be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only going to -- I'm quite content -- it was actually only a guide to what -- we found Mr. McLeod's handwriting - if he won't be too insulted - quite difficult to read, and we had somebody attempt to type it up. It hasn't been done by him and it hasn't been checked by him because there were some difficulties. But I -- I don't know. It may be that Mr. McLeod over the weekend, if he's got nothing better to do, could check the original against the typed version and make the corrections. But at the moment I agree with Mr. Ackerman. I'm quite content only to make the photocopy of the -- the original handwritten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with Mr. Ackerman too, and I would go along with his suggestion. The only thing is that if what has now been suggested by Ms. Korner to Mr. McLeod does not take place, then the fact that we have one page here containing six errors, when compared to the original from which it was copied, is in itself an item of evidence. So -- because if we stay with the original as it is and with the typed version in English as it is, I think we ought to have on record that there is one page containing six -- six errors. That it should be replaced, I agree as well. So this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I leave it? I'll have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- it typed up. If I leave until the Monday, I'll have that particular page retyped by Monday afternoon when we sit again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I just -- I just would like to say that I would be extremely grateful to Mr. McLeod if he would go through that exercise this weekend. And I might even lighten up my cross-examination in payment for that, because I think I'm going to want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- to refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to refer to part of this diary, and if I can't read his handwriting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a question of not being able to read his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's problem number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what may be a bigger problem is the fact that because of that you would rely on the typed version in English that you and I have, and not knowing whether what you're reading is a correct reflection of what is contained -- whether it contains an average of six errors per page, you know, and this is the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Defence is content, what could happen, as I say, and we're trespassing on Mr. McLeod's weekend in Holland --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I know. In fact, I'm not asking him myself --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- but if he were able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because I have no right to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- perhaps on Monday morning we can photocopy the corrections and then retype it at a later stage. If the Defence are happy for someone from the OTP to collect from him on Monday the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. And if it's more convenient for him to do this at his leisure after he leaves here, it could even be done that way. Just at some point during the trial of this case --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- I'd like to have a more accurate version substituted for what you've got in front of you right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGUIS
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. So we take note of that. Of course, the Chamber is not imposing anything on you because you're not responsible for the typed version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could make a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not opposed to, but if I could -- if I could have a copy of the typed version on a disk in Word, I have my computer with me, and I could then come back with the corrected version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure you can put onto a disk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would it be -- do Defence and Your Honours agree that if necessary we can just talk to Mr. McLeod about this aspect of the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Only on this aspect, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that understood and agreed to by the Defence? In other words, the Prosecution is authorised, between now and Monday when -- or Tuesday when we will see Mr. McLeod in this courtroom, that they hand him the typed version in English of -- it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's absolutely fine. No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. So, Mr. McLeod, that brings us to an end just for today. I understand you're in another trial on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. He's back here on Monday, Your Honour. He's giving evidence in the other trial on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Tuesday. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That'll be the sixth trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll meet again -- we'll meet again on Monday, and then you will be cross-examined by the two Defence teams. Thank you. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if there is nothing else, we can adjourn, resuming Monday -- yes. I recognise Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to know if the Prosecution could specify the order that the witnesses will be appearing in next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's the order in which it's now the latest list. The next witness after Mr. McLeod will be 7.112. Then -- yes, 7.119 and then 7.59, I think. Isn't next week a four-day week? I think it is. So I think that will be the only three next week. But after Mr. McLeod, it will be 7.112, 7.119, and then 7.59. I don't think we'll get any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the witness 7.13, isn't that witness not coming next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, on that witness, that's the witness number 27 on the list appearing - the first one - two days ago or -- two days ago, I think, to Monday or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's given evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Cayley told us that there was a rearrangement and that witness BT16 will be called --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 13 was this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. 7.13, yes. He was supposed to have given evidence before --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- before Mr. Biscevic. And I am under the impression that it was either -- it wasn't possible for him to come along or he was not exactly too cooperative or willing to come over, and he would be producing him at a later stage. He couldn't come when --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've been tied up, as Your Honour, I think, knows, in the Stakic case, so I've missed all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is the information that I remember having is from Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'll check with -- yes. I've got an update. Yes. Your Honour, as far as we know, but I hope Ms. Sutherland or Mr. Cayley is watching this and we might get an e-mail correcting this, all I can do is double-check that. All I can say is I do know that the next witness after Mr. McLeod will be 7.112, and I have a feeling -- are we getting any e-mail? Yes, Your Honour. No. 7.13 will be the first week of July. So I think that list that we now have in front of us is the order in which it's running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Does this satisfy you, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry. We had a reminder today that we stated that we put the Rule 92 motion in and we -- I'm afraid to say it's just slipped through the net, but it should be with Your Honours on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witnesses we want to call under Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- and that's -- yes. Can I mention Mr. Mayhew?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honours ruled that he would have been brought for cross-examination though his statement could go in. Can I say that I'm just waiting to see what the cross-examination is here before making a decision whether we require to call him or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. With that, I think we can adjourn. I wish everyone a happy weekend, and we'll resume our labours on Monday in the afternoon. Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of June, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
